Q: Please state your full name for the record.
A: Harry Leo Smith, Jr.

Q: Mr. Smith, I know that you were at Phil Whitaker's deposition a couple of weeks ago, so you're obviously familiar with the deposition process.
A: Uh-huh.

Q: Is that correct?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: And have you ever had your deposition taken?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: How many times?
A: Two to three times.

Q: And you obviously then have been involved in litigation?
A: Mostly mediations.

Q: But you've been sworn under oath to tell the truth?
A: Correct.

Q: Okay. And so you understand that this process today is a deposition in which you're sworn under oath to tell the truth and that I will ask you questions, and you will do the best of your ability to answer those questions honestly and fully?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: And as the court reporter here is taking down everything that's said in the room, it will be very helpful to her if you will answer questions that are posed to you as a yes-no type question, as either yes or no, as opposed to uh-huh or uh-uh or nodding or shaking your head. Do you understand that?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: If at any time you need to take a break, either to use the restroom or get -- get something else to drink or have a discussion with your attorney, will you just let me know that?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: And the only thing that I would ask is that if a question is pending you answer the question first before we take a break.
A: Yes, sir.

Q: Is there any reason that you could not understand questions that I may ask?
A: No, sir.

Q: Okay. And if for some reason you do not understand a question or are confused, will you ask me to repeat that?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: Are you on any medication today?
A: No, sir.

Q: Is there any other reason that you might not be able to understand my questions or to answer truthfully?
A: No, sir.

Q: What have you done to prepare for the deposition today?
A: I had a phone call with my attorney, and I'm obviously familiar with the material.

Q: Other than speaking your attorney, did you speak with anybody else about this deposition?
A: No, sir.

Q: What documents did you review in preparation for this deposition?
A: Well, I've reviewed obviously the non- competes, the buy-out agreements, just from a refreshing standpoint. And I did not review all the e-mails. Once I opened them up, you know, several of those e-mails were not mine and I'm swearing on that in the testimony. And I refused to get past that based on some of the -- what I opened up originally. So, you know, everything else I reviewed in detail.

Q: When you say, "everything else"?
A: The non-competes, the buy-out agreements, the written material that's gone back and forth between the parties.

Q: Okay. And then you said some of the e- mails are not yours?
A: Yeah. The e-mails I opened up that had the pornographic material, you know, I attested that I'd never seen. I've had e-mails of that caliber sent to me over my career, obviously, but I've never seen those e-mails. And so I stopped at that point and didn't open up anything else. I would remember those e-mails. But when I opened up those originals e-mails, I knew they were not mine and I stopped and advised my attorney accordingly.

Q: And we can talk about those later. Let's get into just some preliminary information. What's your date of birth?
A: February 24th, 1970.

Q: What's your home address?
A: 681 VOA Cite C Road, Greenville, North Carolina 27834.

Q: How long have you lived at that address?
A: Approximately 14 years.

Q: And who lives at that address with you?
A: My wife, my son -- and my daughter's at Wake Forest but lives there in the summer.

Q: And you mentioned your wife. How long have you been married?
A: That's a great question. I should answer that quickly, right? I got married in 1994, so whatever the numerics on that are.

Q: And you've only been married once --
A: That's right.

Q: -- to your current wife?
A: Correct.

Q: As far as your education goes, did you graduate from high school in about 1988?
A: Yes, sir. About that.

Q: Where did you graduate from?
A: Clayton High School.

Q: And then you went to college?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: And where did you go?
A: East Carolina University.

Q: When did you graduate from East Carolina University?
A: 1992.

Q: What was your degree in?
A: B.S., B.A., business administration.

Q: Did you do any postgraduate work?
A: No, sir.

Q: Have you had any certifications or training courses that you've undergone?
A: Not in any specificity, no.

Q: After you graduated from East Carolina with a business degree, where did you go to work?
A: I went into distribution and then -- I don't recall the exact years. I spent about four years in distribution.

Q: What company?
A: Cameron and Barkley.

Q: Cameron and Barkley?
A: Yeah.

Q: Where is that located?
A: They were located in Charleston. They had a branch in Greenville. And then they sold out probably three or four different times through those years.

Q: So that was your first place of employment, and you were there for about four years?
A: My very first place of employment was a -- was a company called Industrial Construction, which was also distribution of products. And I was there probably three years. I got recruited to go to Cameron and Barkley and was there approximately three or four years. And then I went in business, you know, really, for myself.

Q: All right. Let me -- let me just go back. With Industrial, the three years you were there, what were you doing?
A: Sales.

Q: Sales of what?
A: MRO supplies, maintenance, repair, operational supplies.

Q: And Cameron and Barkley, what were you doing there?
A: I was a branch Manager, so I ran the branch and performed sales functions as well.

Q: And what were you selling?
A: Same thing, yeah.

Q: Maintenance type supplies?
A: Uh-huh. Yes, sir. MR. GRAY: And let's go off the record just real quick. (Off the record from 9:10 a.m. until 9:11 a.m.) BY MR. GRAY:

Q: After Cameron and Barkley, you said you went into business for yourself?
A: Right. I had -- had my own company, doing sales and marketing. And that's -- I was also sending to and representing Flanders. So that's where my friendship started with Flanders.

Q: Okay. Well, let's -- let's back up just a hair. So you graduated in '92, and you worked for Industrial and Cameron and Barkley for a combined total of about seven to eight years?
A: Six, seven years, something like that, yeah.

Q: So we're getting close to the end of the century?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: And at that point you -- you went in to work for yourself. You went to work for yourself?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: And explain exactly what you were doing?
A: Doing the exact same thing, Ken, but doing it on my own. So, you know, I wanted to, you know, work for myself. So I started a company. I started developing manufacturing relationships where I represented those companies in a sales and -- sales function, selling their products. And I had been doing business -- one of my larger accounts, actually, was Flanders with Industrial Construction and Cameron and Barkley. So -- and that is how -- well, that was one of my lines. I sold air filtration products for Flanders.

Q: Okay. I want to --
A: Not as an employee.

Q: Right. I want to take it step by step here. When you were with Industrial and Cameron and Barkley, explain your relationship with Flanders.
A: Strictly a supplier. So I mean I'd call on those guys and sold them supplies.

Q: And you were selling them maintenance type supplies?
A: Maintenance and OEM type products.

Q: What -- what is that?
A: OEM product would be a product that went into their finished goods. So you may -- you may sell them, you know, electrical wire and conduit for repair in a plant, which we represented. You may sell them a gear or a gear box that went into a finished product. So it would be both products.

Q: You were selling them products that would go into their equipment?
A: Uh-huh. Yes, sir.

Q: Were you -- were you selling them any products that would go into the actual air filtration product that they sold to their customers?
A: Yes. So you would have what we call high purity products, which would be our metal-type products. So we might sell a gear box that went -- that was a permanent mount on that product. But it was just a piece of that product. And then, you know, they have the throw away, which is more your retail products. I didn't sell anything there -- that went into the final product.

Q: How long were you self-employed?
A: Approximately three years or so.

Q: During that time were you doing the same type of -- did you have the same type of relationship with Flanders?
A: I did. But the exception then was I also was representing them. So I -- I got their line and was selling Flanders' products as well. So I had the Flanders' that I was selling. So, you know, I also was -- and when you represent, you have different manufacturers you represent, you know, as either a manufacturer's rep or distributor. And I was able to get the Flanders' products to sell to end users. And I developed that relationship with Pitt Memorial Hospital before it was Vidant. So at that time Robert Amerson, who was the former CEO and Chairman, caught me in the hallway one day and said, Hey, is there anyway you can help us get the Pitt Memorial Hospital business? Now, at this time Flanders is not a large corporation, Ken. And I said, I'd love to -- obviously, right? You know, because I knew it was an opportunity. And I was able to secure that piece of business fairly quickly for Flanders Corporation. You know, Pitt, now Vidant, uses a tremendous amount of filtration, up to and including HEPA filtration. So there's a large range of filtration, right. And so they would use the whole gamut. And that is how the relationship started. I secured that piece of business, and subsequently I was allowed to represent their products going forward.

Q: So during this three-year period in which you were self-employed you were selling products to Flanders --
A: Uh-huh. Yes, sir.

Q: -- for both their machinery and for their end product?
A: Uh-huh. Yes, sir.

Q: And you were also taking the end product and selling it or distributing it to customers?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: Did you have an independent contractor relationship with Flanders at that time?
A: I don't recall. I don't think I had a contract. I think I just had, you know, a verbal agreement that I could represent and sell in a given geographic territory. And back then the company wasn't very complex -- I don't recall if I had a specific contract, but I do not think I did.

Q: And during this period of time when you were self-employed, you were working with other companies as well?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: In terms of selling them products, maintenance type products?
A: Yeah. I was calling on a multitude of companies -- yes, sir.

Q: Were you also selling those other companies' products to customers?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: So what happened to change the relationship between you becoming self-employed and some -- you know, tell me the next step.
A: Robert sat me down one day -- and you know, I was doing fairly well -- and said, I would like for you to come to work for me.

Q: All right. Robert who?
A: Robert Amerson was the CEO and Chairman of Flanders. No, I'm sorry. He was the Chairman, not the CEO. Steve Clark was the CEO. And Robert and I threw it back and forth, and I said, you know, let me think on it. And, you know, he made some appealing -- you know, because I was still young and up and coming, right? And he made some appealing comments to me about leadership in the company, opportunities. And subsequently, you know, he and I came to an agreement that I would actually come to work for the company. So at that time I became an employee of Flanders Corporation.

Q: Do you recall the date?
A: No, sir.

Q: Just ballpark?
A: I really have no idea. I mean I'd love to give you better dates, but it just ran altogether. But I mean I was CEO from -- you can back into it from there. I was CEO from -- call it May of 2007 through '14, I think, 2014. Approximately the same time, Ken, it would be the May time frame period or pretty close. And then prior to that, in a sequence of events, you know, I was Chief Operating Officer of the company. I was --

Q: When were you COO?
A: Approximately a year before I was CEO.

Q: For just a one-year period?
A: Approximately.

Q: So we'll say from about May of 2006 till about May of 2007?
A: Yes, sir, approximately.

Q: Okay. Prior to that point in 2006, when you became the COO, what was your position?
A: I held a number of different positions, from sales to managing direct sales offices, to operations in high purity. So it was just a series of different positions. I moved into the company -- and I basically moved into the company where, you know, we seem to have, you know, financial constraints or financial challenges. And I was moved in those areas accordingly.

Q: Well, okay, but I want to back down. We started with CEO. Then you -- before that you were COO.
A: Uh-huh.

Q: What were you before you were -- immediately before you were COO?
A: Before that I was in charge of high purity operations, high purity sales, and then all commercial sales, except retail.

Q: About how long were you in that position?
A: I don't recall the exact time frame and range. But, you know, I would say a couple years, you know.

Q: So that would put it around the 2004 time period -- from about 2004 to 2006?
A: Approximately, yeah.

Q: Do you recall the position you were in prior to being in charge of the high purity operations?
A: I do. But my original position, Ken, that they brought me into is that I managed the direct office. So Flanders had approximately, probably ten direct offices around the country. And these are actually distributors that we owned. So we had -- the model at that time was, you know, we had direct sales and distribution of sales. So Steve Clark, the CEO, was -- we had direct sales offices, which we owned, which would be 5, 10, 15, 20,000 square feet and a sales force that went out and sold filters. But they were on our payroll. We owned the inventory. And so I ran -- the first thing they did was put me in charge of those direct sales offices. And the assignment was given to me because they were financially challenged. You know, they were having trouble getting them going. And -- but that is the first assignment I got with the company.

Q: Do you recall approximately how long you were in that position?
A: I don't. I'd say 18 months to two years, something like that.

Q: Is it fair to say you started with Flanders somewhere around 2002?
A: Approximately. That's probably fair. I don't recall exactly, but I think you're pretty close.

Q: And to the best of your recollection, you had four different types?
A: That's probably -- probably fair.

Q: The Manager of Direct Offices?
A: Uh-huh.

Q: Director of high purity operations, COO and CEO?
A: Yes, sir. I ran everything at some point in time except retail. I never had retail until I became COO. Then I had retail control as well.

Q: So within those four different roles that you performed you, at one point or the other, oversaw every facet of Flanders' business?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: Mr. Smith, I want to take you to the point of right before you started with Flanders. And you had a relationship for a number of years, it appears a decade relationship as -- you know, working in some type of contractual relationship in terms of providing them with maintenance type materials, and then subsequently in addition to doing that, you were also selling product for Flanders?
A: Uh-huh. Yes, sir.

Q: What was your perception of Flanders?
A: Not a very well run company. You know, when I looked at it, I did see a lot of opportunity. I didn't know much about the air filtration space, but I called on a lot of different people. So, you know, I would call all the billion dollar pharmaceutical companies, obviously a lot of infrastructure very well ran. And I would call small companies, from Hackney and Sons in Washington, that I would probably assimilate along the same lines I would in Flanders at the time, right, which is, you know, undercapitalized, slow pay -- because I got paid slowly. So, you know, I was not -- I never got up in the morning time saying, gee whiz, golly, this is the next best thing since sliced bread. So I didn't have a high perception of the company. I didn't have a low perception of the company. And I also probably wasn't mature enough at that time, Ken, to understand the dynamics of the capitalization and finance like I do now. So -- but I don't recall having some -- you know a great perception of it. I mean my perception at that time, based on use and experience, was, you know, when I went into a big pharmaceutical company, it enamored me. And then when I went to Little Washington, not so much.

Q: And Little Washington is where Flanders is based?
A: Was headquartered at that time, yes, sir.

Q: Did you call on any other air filtration companies prior to going to work for Flanders?
A: I attempted to. I tried to do business with Purolater, as I recall. I don't recall anybody else that I tried to -- I was really kind of geographically -- you know, Eastern North Carolina. I had some products that I thought that I could have sold in other markets, but I was not successful in doing it.

Q: Were you aware of Flanders' competitors at the time, before you went to work for Flanders?
A: I was aware of a few, but had no idea of the range of competitors. So I would tell you my knowledge was limited as to the breadth and depth of who could do what in the space.

Q: Once you began your employment with Flanders, did that knowledge base change?
A: Dramatically.

Q: How so?
A: Well, you know, I think ingrained myself in the business, you know, based on what, you know, I was perceived and was told as an economic opportunity for me. And I quickly learned, you know, the landscape, you know, and it's multifaceted. So, you know, you have retail, which is obviously big box stores. You have what we call ARW, which is air conditioner, refrigeration and wholesale, which would be like your Johnstone Supplies, C.C. Dixons, which would be a local distributor to sell fans, belts, freon, air filters. So the mechanical contractors you would call here today, he would go by there and pick up a can of freon, he'd get a case of filters. So that's a space. And then we have the filter sales and service space, which would be Ken Gray owns Ken Gray Filters Sales and Service. You have the warehouse, two trucks. And you call on hospitals, pharmaceuticals and plants locally. And you would buy our products and sell our products. So that's the third space. And, you know, we had the high purity space, which is HEPA filtration, clean room filtration and nuclear filtration. And then, you know, we had a complete service division, which was rooftop change outs, mostly big box stores, so forth and so on. And we also had a paint booth division. So the paint booth division would sell paint booth and roll type products to, you know, automobile dealerships and so forth. And so, you know, what I learned quickly was it was a pretty complex model. And so I really ingrained myself into learning, who, what, when where and how from a competitive landscape. So I would say, yeah, I got up to speed really, really quickly on -- on all the divisions.

Q: Okay. Let me go through --
A: And I'm sorry, retail as well.

Q: Yeah. Retail, explain that. And basically explain what Flanders does.
A: Sure. Yeah. So Flanders Corporation, you know, is a multi-faceted air filtration company. What I got at Flanders Corporation is an evolution of the model. So when I got to Flanders Corporation it was in financial challenge. It's public record was a NASDAQ traded company. So what my thesis when they offered me -- took the job, was that we had a model problem. Because, you know, we had the direct offices I was telling you about, and then, you know, we also sold to Ken Gray Filter Sales and Service. So you would actually go and compete with our direct offices every day. So we'd have sales guys on our payroll competing with you selling our products. And the same thing in the retail space. Instead of you going to Lowe's, you could just go to one of our direct offices and buy our filters. So, you know, what I said is we had a confused strategy. And what we had at that time was a CEO that was buying (indiscernible.) So I mean, he was losing market share in the normalized market because people didn't trust us as a partner, because we were competing with him. Q: During your tenure as CEO?
A: During my tenure, but we were not the leader in that space. In high purity I would tell you we were the leader domestically, not internationally. But in the United States, you know, I felt like we had a predominant market share. We attempted to open in Europe, and I was unsuccessful. I was unable to make it go.

Q: In high purity?
A: Yes, sir. I put a couple people over there and we started talking about manufacturing plants, people, place and things. It's a totally different structure in how they operate. I did not have, one, enough time; two, enough capital. So I -- I -- I gave it about a year trying to figure it out. Part of my strategy there was to exit. Because if we were going to sell the company, we were also selling opportunities. And I wanted to show that market is an opportunity. I could never get traction and I retracted. So as I exited, we were very much the predominant player in three spaces, in my opinion.

Q: And you mentioned the largest manufacturer of air filtration in the country; is that correct?
A: Yes, that's correct.

Q: How did that compare to the world?
A: I don't know what the world space is. That's a great question. I mean I've heard numbers. I don't know if I recall anything. But, you know, we were at a run rate of 325 or 335 when I exited. Q: And what do you attribute the success of Flanders going from not being the leader in any of those areas to it being the leader in at least three of those areas that you talked about?
A: -Team. And we ran a really fun, upbeat, fast company. I was over engaged in the company. It was a mistake of mine. At the age I was and you put what you put in, you get over engaged.

Q: And when you say it was a mistake, you're talking about from a health standpoint?

At some point you gotta go. And we'll talk about it when we get to that point on the dynamics of why I left. But I -- you know, I -- I -- I was all in and I had a team that was all in. And I led -- I was heavily involved in sales. I was heavily involved in the procurement of the vendor base, driving cost out, you know, worked with vendors. I was very involved with customers -- I mean employees. You know, I made sure I visited plants, talked to people, walked. And so I would tell you from that standpoint I was over engaged. Because at the point when it came -- I got the company where I wanted to. But then when I was trying to figure out how to get out, it got tough.

Q: Were you the primary individual who led to the success of Flanders becoming a market leader?
A: You know, without making an egotistical statement, there's no doubt. And I think Insight will tell you the same thing, and so would my Board of Directors. And I think the customers, vendors and employees would tell you that.

Q: Were you the one at Flanders with the primary customer relationship with the most important customers?
A: Absolutely.

Q: And I think you mentioned those previously, but that's Home Depot --
A: Yes. And I'll name what I would -- and there's a lot of -- everybody's key and critical. But, you know, when I got up in the morning time, I looked at it as though you can't -- we can't lose these. So these are the can't-lose-accounts. So it would be Home Depot. It would have been Grainger. It would have been ACE. It would have been Wal- Mart. It would have been Johnstone supply on the ARW side. It would have been C.C. Dixon. It would have been the Ware Group. Q: And of those eight to ten entities that you just named, what percentage of the business do you think that accounted for?
A: I think if you're 335, I think that's 200. It's the number I put in the e-mail to Phil. I mean I think if I went in the space that I -- I mean I'm not -- in total transparency, I think I could absolutely move those customers. I'm not denying that. I think I would have a percent success in moving those customers.

Q: In other words, just to be clear, I think what you just are -- testified to was that if you went into competition with Flanders right now, you'd be able to get virtually all of that eight to ten -- those eight to ten entities, which you equate to about $200 million?
A: I feel that way. And so, you know, I'm not going to -- obviously, I'm not going to mislead you. I mean I feel that way. And, you know, that's predicated on a couple of different fronts. So, you know, why did I exit? One, I was incredibly tired. Two, I wanted to take the chips off the table. I mean, you know, mitigate risk. And, three, I had gotten everything I thought I could get out of it without really hunkering down for another five years, right. So I thought margins were going to be depressed, you know, on the retail side. I thought there was potential to lose market share from a destruction player. My biggest concern was the scale and magnitude of the model with entry level labor. And so when I looked at the model, you know, we were 4,000 employees, a great big number, 85 percent at your entry level labor. So we had built a model on entry level labor, that I also was seeing a shortage of. So we started, you know, having trouble filling plants, getting positions that -- you know, it started concerning me. Because you can't run a model without entry level labor. Now, we started developing automation, which we developed in-house. Okay, slow down -- we started developing automation that we developed internally, and it was a booming success. But it still wasn't enough that you had to have significant entry level labor. So when I looked at the model, we had too many plants and, you know, not enough entry level labor. And I felt like, you know, we needed a massive amount of capital to fully automate the plants. So I just said, look, it's time for me to mitigate my risks and exit. And, you know, I was -- I was pretty open about that. And I also thought the right player could grow the business with the right capital structure. And so I encouraged Insight that it was time to exit. And on one point I'm going to go back, because this is a critical point on two phases. This kind of ties Pronamics in. And I will tie it together in three minutes. So one of the issues -- or five minutes, Ken. One of the issues we had with Home Depot was 3M was manufacturing their own media. So they had proprietary media. So one of the reasons we were able to get Home Depot was we had found a company in South Carolina called ECN Industries. And the guy's name was Rick Chapman. And he was operating in a small, eight or 10,000 square foot building. And we stumbled upon Rick, and Rick actually had developed the number one performing media in air filtration, one guy, a brainiac. Couldn't carry on a conversation, knew everything about air filtration media. We took that as part of our package to Home Depot and is one of the reasons we were able to displace 3M. Because we had a media that actually beat 3Ms proprietary media. So went back to Insight and said, we've got to protect this product. And so Insight said, you know, we agree. We think that we should be in the media business as 3M is. We don't want to deploy anymore capital, because we want to exit. Will you help us? I had an incredible relationship with Home Depot. I made a mistake. I put my capital in, bought ECN with the Board's support. And we became Pronamics. That's how Pronamics was formed, is we bought ECN, which had the proprietary media to service Home Depot. So we had -- that is how Pronamics came about.

Q: All right. Let me stop you there.
A: Sure.

Q: When you say, "we bought ECN," who is we?
A: So it would have been myself, Kevin Boyd, and John Paul Corey. So I had 65 percent ownership. Kevin had 25 and John Paul had 15. And John Paul was learning from Rick and learning the operation, because Rick had some age on him. And, you know, Kevin was helping us build equipment to enhance what Rick had. Rick was under capitalized, had one piece of equipment. We needed more.

Q: So when you -- the three of you bought ECN Industries, at that point you renamed it Pronamics?
A: Correct. Correct. We renamed it. Went to Home Depot. And then we developed a plan alongside Home Depot, Insight and ourselves to buy two pieces of equipment to supply Home Depot. Because we were having service issues. Rick couldn't run enough media, and then he had a down issue, I believe, one time and we -- we -- we collapsed Home Depot in the summertime. And as a part of Pronamics, we had -- this is how the fiberglass operation started. We had a relationship with a company called Superior Fibers. When I became CEO, the former CEO had gotten into the media business and had bought two pieces of equipment and opened the Clarkton, North Carolina, that made MERV 6, 7 and 8, which is your very entry level media. And when we were exiting anything that was not core, I spun that business off to our fiberglass supplier, Superior Fibers. We bought all our fiberglass air filtration media from them. And so we helped them get in that media business to help round the model up, and we exited. How we ended up in the fiberglass media business was Superior Fibers shut down one of their main facilities and attempted to move it to Mexico. And it caused a catastrophic supply chain shortage. The plant was a colossal failure and they closed it. But we had a massive void in raw material that was key and critical to Flanders. So, again, we sat down as a Board with Insight and I said, we have to -- you know, what do we do here? We decided that we would start manufacturing our own fiberglass media. And, again --

You know, we didn't worry about making payroll. We were a lot more current with the vendor base. I will tell you we never fully paid the vendor base on time, you know, when I was the CEO. So if you had a 30-day term, we probably paid you 45. And -- but that went from -- we had 30-day terms and we paid you at 120, which is when I got it. And so that was a lot of communication with the vendor base. But we still didn't have millions in capital, so we were building the company. So we were creating EBITDA, investing in equipment to try to grow revenues. I think I can prove it out pretty quickly and I think the actions will show it on business stopping without explanation, raw materials we had and carried that we ate, so forth and so on. You know, I've gotten significant comments back from key and critical people and comments made in staff meetings, you know, about me. I think people have been terminated as a result of me. It's the reason I didn't depose anybody else because I didn't want anybody else to lose their job. Look, Ken, this is not a thing where I have any desire to -- here's what I don't want. I don't want my obviously challenged relationship with Phil Whitaker, okay, and there's no doubt it is. And I tried to take that because I made some mistakes in that and I admit those. I should have continued to rise above it, I regret it. I don't want my angst with this guy, and it's one of the reasons I reached out to his supervision, I don't want my angst with this guy to hurt the company, right. And so, I want to be cognitive of that, right? And so, I want to rise above that. And then also is the reason I apologized to Phil because I thought I owed him that. And, you know, so I tried to go back to where I started this thing is can we help you. And so, I don't think the company should get hurt because me and this guy are banging it out. I actually would like to see this guy be successful. And so, if I can help -- and look, by the way, if they say here, this is what you're missing and this is why the people are calling you and, you know, you're wrong here, I would love to hear that because I could be. I don't -- I don't think I am based on what I'm seeing and I'm hearing but I could be. Some of that stuff is going to be what it's going to be, right? But, you know, I don't want to do that. I mean look, I just -- I don't want to do that. And so, you know, as much as emotions in this thing for me and by the way, it is, and I've always said separate your emotions and your business making skills, I've got some emotional decisions in this that I regret. You know, in my journey through life I looked at that said, you know, it was a mistake by me. I'm willing today to take Phil to McDonalds and say how can I help you and continue the apology path. So, you know, because I do. I mean I reacted I think. But I mean look, I don't -- I don't want to go in the air filtration business. I feel like I'm being forced into it. And maybe I'm wrong about that, right. But I'm not going to leave here today doing back flips thinking I'm getting back in. As I've told Kevin all along, right, I've been there.

Q: . Don't say anything you've told your attorney.
A: . Yeah, okay. But I mean, you know, I've been there. This is full disclosure. I mean listen, we can do this process, that process, what I've done today is total transparency, right? And, you know, I want to see the company be successful. I want to see it flourish in North Carolina specifically, I don't deny that. And I'm not crazy about going back in air filtration. I'm really not. In fact, I don't want to go back in air filtration. I feel like I'm being forced back in air filtration.

Q: . Who's forcing you?
A: . I feel like I'm -- I have a responsibility customers, vendors, and employees. You know, I feel like my two main guys who don't care to go back in air filtration either have been attacked and harmed financially. I think they have some emotions on it on how they feel like they've been treated. I mean two great guys that gave nothing but time, energy, and effort to the company and exited with grace, style, and dignity. I mean when you have an exit like that there's some emotions, right? But at the end of the day we all -- I took it up there, we took it up there, we worked through and, you know, and we ended up all in a good place. And so, you know, for whatever reason this thing started off on the wrong track and it started off with actions against us. And what I would have done is said hey, let me call those guys in so I can understand everything that happened because I've been told this, what's your story. Travis, Kevin, and myself would have sat down with Phil and said hey, whatever we can do to help you. By the way, you want me to go to Home Depot with you and introduce those guys, let's go next week. So, I mean we would have all done that. That offer's still there, right? I mean, you know, I mean can we build a machine? Like you've never seen. I mean Kevin, who owns Oak Ridge, designed every piece of equipment air filtration, right? He's got the shop to build it in. We built it low cost, right? He's happy, Travis is happy, I'm really happy. It's not what I want to do. So, I'm not -- I don't -- I don't -- that's not what I want to do. And I feel like -- I feel like I have a responsibility to people that, you know, did a lot for me.

Q: . One thing you mentioned not as a reason is money. You don't need the money, do you?
A: . I don't need the money. You know, and I'll speak authoritatively on that subject. So, you're talking about a guy came from nothing, right? Graduated from East Carolina broke. And, you know, I've built a significant net worth. Outside of Flanders as well I've had significant success. And so, you know, I have a fair -- I mean I would say enormous but a lot of wealth. So, I have no desire to go back in the -- I don't need any more, right? I mean I just don't need any more money. What I do want is my time. And so, you know, when I speak on that subject, I really wanted to do civic stuff and take the stuff that I learned and the mistakes I made in business and in life, and I've got them, to the civic side of things and that's what I've done, you know, as you're aware on the Board of Governors. I've taken that skill set and by the way I've had some tremendous success for the system. And so, I enjoy that process. I mean, you know, pay's not good but I've enjoyed the process. And, you know, and that's really what I'd like to do. Do I have some political ambitions? Ken, I do, and I think I'll have success there, right? I haven't vetted that out yet but it's part of the reason I wanted to stay in higher education. So, I've got things that I want to do. This thing will take three or four years of my life away from me. So, I don't need any more money. I really enjoy my time and I want to be able to go watch ACC soccer, I want to be able to go to football games. It is -- and by the way, my guys feel the same way. So, Travis has got a highly successful business. I own half of it, it does really well. Kevin now has taken Oak Ridge it's doing really well. So, I mean you're talking about guys that own pretty nice businesses, you know, 20 million, 10 million that make nice -- I mean they're fine. They don't need any more money either. And so we -- those two guys with me made a massive push and got that thing where it was at. And, you know, we feel like we've been attacked, we feel like we've been defamed. I think that's true. We got customers, vendors, and employees calling us. I will repeat to you again I've made mistakes, I regret them. Phil Whitaker said last week Mr. Smith can take 200 million hire employees, people, place, and things. He's correct about that. I left there, I slept, prayed on it, talked to my wife about it. I said I'm going to do the right thing here. I sent him an apology which was meaningful. I made a mistake, I wanted to correct it. I furthered that with I'll cease and desist and come help you for free. If he genuinely believed and I think he does, then somebody at Daikin's Board ought to say hold on a second here, if you believe this guy can build a $200 million business, he's offered to help you for free and stop. So, who's at fault here, right? And by the way, he could have also ,said Harry, I don't want your help but I'm going to ask you to stop, and by the way, I owe you an apology, and he does, for things that I did and actions I've taken against people, place, and things with you, I would have accepted his apology, right? If he'd said, Harry, this is what I'm going to do to fix the company so people quit calling you, probably could have left there that day, Ken, and went back to studying budget and finance for the next Board of Governors meeting. So, you know, I don't want to hurt this company by hurting him. Is that -- is that fair? I just want the company to be successful. I don't -- I don't -- I don't want anybody to say that I've got some massive pretense to crush Flanders and go in the air filtration business. I'm here today. I spent a significant amount of money to validate my name, to validate my guys' name and to protect people that were very important to me that I think are being hurt. I think the performance of the company will prove that, right? That's all I care about. I -- I -- I -- that's all I care about. I mean, you know, and I'm telling you this guy did take action against me and my guys. It's very provable. And there was comments made about us. It's very provable. The performance of the company is falling. Jobs are being lost. People are scared, right, people that were deemed to be aligned with me have been terminated, let go, or punished. That's all provable. I don't understand why but I -- I -- I want to help. If they don't want my help then and that's fine, you know, somebody get it on track. And I'll go back to sending you guys post cards, right? It's the only reason that I didn't want you guys not to have this engagement because win, lose, or draw you should have it. I mean you guys -- I mean so -- because I mean I think it comes down to case law. So, I'm not going to hurt anybody. One of the biggest problems I've had with this thing was people got hurt because of me. There are people that have lost this job since I filed this lawsuit a hundred percent because they will prove -- they were thought to be aligned with me. There are people that I've known for 20- plus years, their families, wives, daughters, went to their kids' graduation, grew up with them, that are afraid to talk to me today because they think they'll be fired just for communicating with me, right? I mean there is a context in the company if you're aligned with Harry, you get fired. And his actions prove that. He's fired people because they're aligned with me. That's why I didn't depose anybody. We had stuff we could bring the table, Ken, and we stopped. I had people I could have brought to this table that would have had significant testimony and I stopped because I don't want anybody else hurt. MR. GRAY: Do you have any questions? MR. CEGLOWSKI: Are you done? MR. GRAY: For this part. C R O S S E X A M I N A T I O N2:40 P.M. BY MR. CEGLOWSKI:

Q: . Mr. Smith, I'm going to pull back up briefly Exhibit 26, which is the Agreement at issue in the case, the primary one, the Equity Buy-Out and Board of Directors Resignation Agreement.
A: . Uh-huh.

Q: . I just want to be clear for the record at some point you were holding or touching this document and also talking at the sale of the glass plant and Pronamics.
A: . Uh-huh.

Q: . Did that document, Exhibit 26, have any connection to the sale of Pronamics?
A: . None whatsoever. Two totally separate transactions.

Q: . Did that document have any connection to the sale of any business?
A: . None whatsoever. And Insight will testify accordingly.

Q: . Mr. Smith, do I understand your testimony to be that one of your motivations for pursuing this lawsuit is to stop people from being hurt, specifically customers, vendors, and employees of Flanders Corporation?
A: . That's correct.

Q: . Is it true that based on the current dynamic between you and Phil Whitaker and/or you and Flanders the only way for your stop them getting hurt is to reenter the air filtration industry? MR. GRAY: Objection to the form of these questions. They're all leading. THE WITNESS: I believe that -- that is absolutely correct. I feel like I'm being forced back into air filtration to -- on multiple fronts to vindicate my name in the company, Travis Stephenson's name in the company, Kevin Boyd's name in the company, to vindicate personal actions taken against Oak Ridge and Pitt, which are provable, and to stop the flow of business as immediate as the transactions. We can also prove that the decisions made to move business from Oak Ridge were a financial detriment to the company and were personal in nature. I think you will find out that the actions that Phil Whitaker has taken have been personal in nature. I also will tell you that -- and I was told by Insight that there was never a question asked about my non-compete in any way, shape, form, or fashion when they bought the company. Nobody asked about it, they never referred to it. And exactly what Brad Buser told me is there's some attorney somewhere in a back room that saw it but your name never came up, you were not an issue. They bought the company without ever worrying about you. I can also tell you that I was told by -- by a great source that they had to scramble to find my non-compete and figure what it was all about. But the premise of the thing is, you know, I'm here today to validate myself, Travis, Kevin, and people, place, and things that helped me be successful that I think are under attack. And I think people specifically that it is deemed or aligned with me that he has taken personal action again. And I think that's all provable. BY MR. CEGLOWSKI: . Is it important to you to have the flexibility to reenter the air filtration industry if you choose to do so?
A: . Absolutely, yeah. I mean I -- you know -- my main premise would be to see the company be successful and me not enter the air filtration business. If the people that -- that know me and that are perceived to be aligned with me, you know, are not under threat or fear of intimidation because of their alignment with me, and they don't have to worry about coming to work, that the attacks on me stop and the attacks on people, place, and things stop then, you know, I have no desire to enter the air filtration business.

Q: . Is it important to you to have guidance from the court in this case about whether or not the non-compete is enforceable?
A: . Absolutely.

Q: . And do you need that clarity so that you can decide whether or not to reenter the air filtration business?
A: . Absolutely. I mean, you know, I -- again last week I think I led in the fact that I issued an apology. I think -- I think this whole thing precipitated on attacks. I didn't lead that, you know, I responded to it. Over a long period of time it continued and it's continued. And so, you know, my attempt last week was an attempt to peel that divide, rise above that, issue Phil a personal apology, and to also give him an opportunity on the comment on the $200 million company and hiring people to offer not to do that. And if he feels that way, then obviously he feels like I have a tremendous amount of knowledge that he doesn't have and the industry doesn't have or I couldn't do that to bring that knowledge to them free of charge and they've chosen not to act on that. I'm happy to help them today. MR. CEGLOWSKI: I don't have any more questions. R E D I R E C T E X A M I N A T I O N 2:43 p.m. BY MR. GRAY:

Q: . Mr. Smith, you just said it was important to you to have flexibility to enter the air filtration business. Was it important to you when you signed this Equity Buy-out Agreement on March 20th, 2015?
A: . No, and, you know, at that time, you know, what I discussed openly with Insight is treat me with dignity and respect, treat my guys with dignity and respect, and, you know, I'm here to help you forever and they did that.

Q: . And you also testified that it was important for you to have the court make a determination as to the enforceability of the Non- Compete Agreement and the Equity Buy-Out. Was that same thing important to you on March 20th, 2015?
A: . I wasn't under attack, my guys weren't under attack, and I wasn't getting calls from customers, vendors, and employees, people had not lost their job as a result of alignment with me. So, that was not an issue. I will testify again I have no desire to go back in the air filtration business in in any way, shape, form, or fashion.

Q: . So, the answer is no, it was not important at that time?
A: . Absolutely not. I will also say as far as an air filtration start up I mean, you know, I'm three years now so I got two years left, 24 months and now really isn't going to make any difference if they don't change the model. But what I will you is no matter what the court decides if something doesn't change course, Kevin and Travis are going to reenter the space. Their non-competes are clear and they going to have the same kind of impact. I don't know the magnitude of the impact, but I think those guys will have a significant impact whether I'm involved or not. So, you know, Travis and Kevin are completely cleared and I think you'll see unless something changes, those guys will enter the space and -- on their own without me in any way, shape, form, or fashion. That's I think -- I think that's what will happen if something doesn't change course. MR. GRAY: Anything else? MR. CEGLOWSKI: No. MR. GRAY: Let's go off the record. (Off the record 2:46 p.m. until 2:48 p.m.) MR. GRAY: I have no further questions that are not going to be subject to the protective order that we're getting ready to stipulate to. Do you have any additional questions, Kevin? MR. CEGLOWSKI: I do not. MR. GRAY: Okay. At this time we're going to go through a few emails and there is a protective order that's been entered by the court to keep these documents confidential and just not to be distributed beyond the parties. And so, this next section -- the remainder of the deposition will be subject to that protective order. (The following pages numbered 251 - 257 were designated confidential by agreement of counsel.) (These pages were redacted and deleted from this transcript to be filed as CONFIDENTIAL/) (End of confidential portion of transcript.) MR. GRAY: I have no further questions. MR. I would remember those e-mails. But when I opened up those originals e-mails, I knew they were not mine and I stopped and advised my attorney accordingly.

ou been married?

A: Correct.

Q: What company?
A: Cameron and Barkley.

Q: Cameron and Barkley?
A: Yeah.

Q: Where is that located?
A: They were located in Charleston. They had a branch in Greenville. And then they sold out probably three or four different times through those years.

Q: So that was your first place of employment, and you were there for about four years?
A: My very first place of employment was a -- was a company called Industrial Construction, which was also distribution of products. And I was there probably three years. I got recruited to go to Cameron and Barkley and was there approximately three or four years. And then I went in business, you know, really, for myself.

Q: All right. Let me -- let me just go back. With Industrial, the three years you were there, what were you doing?
A: Sales.

Q: Sales of what?
A: MRO supplies, maintenance, repair, operational supplies.

Q: And Cameron and Barkley, what were you doing there?
A: I was a branch Manager, so I ran the branch and performed sales functions as well.

Q: And what were you selling?
A: Same thing, yeah.

Q: Maintenance type supplies?
A: Uh-huh. Yes, sir. MR. GRAY: And let's go off the record just real quick. (Off the record from 9:10 a.m. until 9:11 a.m.) BY MR. GRAY:

Q: After Cameron and Barkley, you said you went into business for yourself?
A: Right. I had -- had my own company, doing sales and marketing. And that's -- I was also sending to and representing Flanders. So that's where my friendship started with Flanders.

Q: Okay. Well, let's -- let's back up just a hair. So you graduated in '92, and you worked for Industrial and Cameron and Barkley for a combined total of about seven to eight years?
A: Six, seven years, something like that, yeah.

Q: So we're getting close to the end of the century?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: And at that point you -- you went in to work for yourself. You went to work for yourself?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: And explain exactly what you were doing?
A: Doing the exact same thing, Ken, but doing it on my own. So, you know, I wanted to, you know, work for myself. So I started a company. I started developing manufacturing relationships where I represented those companies in a sales and -- sales function, selling their products. And I had been doing business -- one of my larger accounts, actually, was Flanders with Industrial Construction and Cameron and Barkley. So -- and that is how -- well, that was one of my lines. I sold air filtration products for Flanders.

Q: Okay. I want to --
A: Not as an employee.

Q: Right. I want to take it step by step here. When you were with Industrial and Cameron and Barkley, explain your relationship with Flanders.
A: Strictly a supplier. So I mean I'd call on those guys and sold them supplies.

Q: And you were selling them maintenance type supplies?
A: Maintenance and OEM type products.

Q: What -- what is that?
A: OEM product would be a product that went into their finished goods. So you may -- you may sell them, you know, electrical wire and conduit for repair in a plant, which we represented. You may sell them a gear or a gear box that went into a finished product. So it would be both products.
08_chunk_0002.title: 08 (chunk 3/56)

08_chunk_0003.text:
ay sell them, you know, electrical wire and conduit for repair in a plant, which we represented. You may sell them a gear or a gear box that went into a finished product. So it would be both products.

Q: You were selling them products that would go into their equipment?
A: Uh-huh. Yes, sir.

Q: Were you -- were you selling them any products that would go into the actual air filtration product that they sold to their customers?
A: Yes. So you would have what we call high purity products, which would be our metal-type products. So we might sell a gear box that went -- that was a permanent mount on that product. But it was just a piece of that product. And then, you know, they have the throw away, which is more your retail products. I didn't sell anything there -- that went into the final product.

Q: How long were you self-employed?
A: Approximately three years or so.

Q: During that time were you doing the same type of -- did you have the same type of relationship with Flanders?
A: I did. But the exception then was I also was representing them. So I -- I got their line and was selling Flanders' products as well. So I had the Flanders' that I was selling. So, you know, I also was -- and when you represent, you have different manufacturers you represent, you know, as either a manufacturer's rep or distributor. And I was able to get the Flanders' products to sell to end users. And I developed that relationship with Pitt Memorial Hospital before it was Vidant. So at that time Robert Amerson, who was the former CEO and Chairman, caught me in the hallway one day and said, Hey, is there anyway you can help us get the Pitt Memorial Hospital business? Now, at this time Flanders is not a large corporation, Ken. And I said, I'd love to -- obviously, right? You know, because I knew it was an opportunity. And I was able to secure that piece of business fairly quickly for Flanders Corporation. You know, Pitt, now Vidant, uses a tremendous amount of filtration, up to and including HEPA filtration. So there's a large range of filtration, right. And so they would use the whole gamut. And that is how the relationship started. I secured that piece of business, and subsequently I was allowed to represent their products going forward.

Q: So during this three-year period in which you were self-employed you were selling products to Flanders --
A: Uh-huh. Yes, sir.

Q: -- for both their machinery and for their end product?
A: Uh-huh. Yes, sir.

Q: And you were also taking the end product and selling it or distributing it to customers?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: Did you have an independent contractor relationship with Flanders at that time?
A: I don't recall. I don't think I had a contract. I think I just had, you know, a verbal agreement that I could represent and sell in a given geographic territory. And back then the company wasn't very complex -- I don't recall if I had a specific contract, but I do not think I did.

Q: And during this period of time when you were self-employed, you were working with other companies as well?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: In terms of selling them products, maintenance type products?
A: Yeah. I was calling on a multitude of companies -- yes, sir.

Q: Were you also selling those other companies' products to customers?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: So what happened to change the relationship between you becoming self-employed and some -- you know, tell me the next step.
A: Robert sat me down one day -- and you know, I was doing fairly well -- and said, I would like for you to come to work for me.

Q: All right. Robert who?
A: Robert Amerson was the CEO and Chairman of Flanders. No, I'm sorry. He was the Chairman, not the CEO. Steve Clark was the CEO. And Robert and I threw it back and forth, and I said, you know, let me think on it. And, you know, he made some appealing -- you know, because I was still young and up and coming, right? And he made some appealing comments to me about leadership in the company, opportunities. And subsequently, you know, he and I came to an agreement that I would actually come to work for the company. So at that time I became an employee of Flanders Corporation.
08_chunk_0003.title: 08 (chunk 4/56)

08_chunk_0004.text:
the company, opportunities. And subsequently, you know, he and I came to an agreement that I would actually come to work for the company. So at that time I became an employee of Flanders Corporation.

Q: Do you recall the date?
A: No, sir.

Q: Just ballpark?
A: I really have no idea. I mean I'd love to give you better dates, but it just ran altogether. But I mean I was CEO from -- you can back into it from there. I was CEO from -- call it May of 2007 through '14, I think, 2014. Approximately the same time, Ken, it would be the May time frame period or pretty close. And then prior to that, in a sequence of events, you know, I was Chief Operating Officer of the company. I was --

Q: When were you COO?
A: Approximately a year before I was CEO.

Q: For just a one-year period?
A: Approximately.

Q: So we'll say from about May of 2006 till about May of 2007?
A: Yes, sir, approximately.

Q: Okay. Prior to that point in 2006, when you became the COO, what was your position?
A: I held a number of different positions, from sales to managing direct sales offices, to operations in high purity. So it was just a series of different positions. I moved into the company -- and I basically moved into the company where, you know, we seem to have, you know, financial constraints or financial challenges. And I was moved in those areas accordingly.

Q: Well, okay, but I want to back down. We started with CEO. Then you -- before that you were COO.
A: Uh-huh.

Q: What were you before you were -- immediately before you were COO?
A: Before that I was in charge of high purity operations, high purity sales, and then all commercial sales, except retail.

Q: About how long were you in that position?
A: I don't recall the exact time frame and range. But, you know, I would say a couple years, you know.

Q: So that would put it around the 2004 time period -- from about 2004 to 2006?
A: Approximately, yeah.

Q: Do you recall the position you were in prior to being in charge of the high purity operations?
A: I do. But my original position, Ken, that they brought me into is that I managed the direct office. So Flanders had approximately, probably ten direct offices around the country. And these are actually distributors that we owned. So we had -- the model at that time was, you know, we had direct sales and distribution of sales. So Steve Clark, the CEO, was -- we had direct sales offices, which we owned, which would be 5, 10, 15, 20,000 square feet and a sales force that went out and sold filters. But they were on our payroll. We owned the inventory. And so I ran -- the first thing they did was put me in charge of those direct sales offices. And the assignment was given to me because they were financially challenged. You know, they were having trouble getting them going. And -- but that is the first assignment I got with the company.

Q: Do you recall approximately how long you were in that position?
A: I don't. I'd say 18 months to two years, something like that.

Q: Is it fair to say you started with Flanders somewhere around 2002?
A: Approximately. That's probably fair. I don't recall exactly, but I think you're pretty close.

Q: And to the best of your recollection, you had four different types?
A: That's probably -- probably fair.

Q: The Manager of Direct Offices?
A: Uh-huh.

Q: Director of high purity operations, COO and CEO?
A: Yes, sir. I ran everything at some point in time except retail. I never had retail until I became COO. Then I had retail control as well.

Q: So within those four different roles that you performed you, at one point or the other, oversaw every facet of Flanders' business?
A: Yes, sir.

Q: Mr. Smith, I want to take you to the point of right before you started with Flanders. And you had a relationship for a number of years, it appears a decade relationship as -- you know, working in some type of contractual relationship in terms of providing them with maintenance type materials, and then subsequently in addition to doing that, you were also selling product for Flanders?
A: Uh-huh. Yes, sir.
08_chunk_0004.title: 08 (chunk 5/56)

08_chunk_0005.text:
f contractual relationship in terms of providing them with maintenance type materials, and then subsequently in addition to doing that, you were also selling product for Flanders?
A: Uh-huh. Yes, sir.

Q: What was your perception of Flanders?
A: Not a very well run company. You know, when I looked at it, I did see a lot of opportunity. I didn't know much about the air filtration space, but I called on a lot of different people. So, you know, I would call all the billion dollar pharmaceutical companies, obviously a lot of infrastructure very well ran. And I would call small companies, from Hackney and Sons in Washington, that I would probably assimilate along the same lines I would in Flanders at the time, right, which is, you know, undercapitalized, slow pay -- because I got paid slowly. So, you know, I was not -- I never got up in the morning time saying, gee whiz, golly, this is the next best thing since sliced bread. So I didn't have a high perception of the company. I didn't have a low perception of the company. And I also probably wasn't mature enough at that time, Ken, to understand the dynamics of the capitalization and finance like I do now. So -- but I don't recall having some -- you know a great perception of it. I mean my perception at that time, based on use and experience, was, you know, when I went into a big pharmaceutical company, it enamored me. And then when I went to Little Washington, not so much.

Q: And Little Washington is where Flanders is based?
A: Was headquartered at that time, yes, sir.

Q: Did you call on any other air filtration companies prior to going to work for Flanders?
A: I attempted to. I tried to do business with Purolater, as I recall. I don't recall anybody else that I tried to -- I was really kind of geographically -- you know, Eastern North Carolina. I had some products that I thought that I could have sold in other markets, but I was not successful in doing it.

Q: Were you aware of Flanders' competitors at the time, before you went to work for Flanders?
A: I was aware of a few, but had no idea of the range of competitors. So I would tell you my knowledge was limited as to the breadth and depth of who could do what in the space.

Q: Once you began your employment with Flanders, did that knowledge base change?
A: Dramatically.

Q: How so?
A: Well, you know, I think ingrained myself in the business, you know, based on what, you know, I was perceived and was told as an economic opportunity for me. And I quickly learned, you know, the landscape, you know, and it's multifaceted. So, you know, you have retail, which is obviously big box stores. You have what we call ARW, which is air conditioner, refrigeration and wholesale, which would be like your Johnstone Supplies, C.C. Dixons, which would be a local distributor to sell fans, belts, freon, air filters. So the mechanical contractors you would call here today, he would go by there and pick up a can of freon, he'd get a case of filters. So that's a space. And then we have the filter sales and service space, which would be Ken Gray owns Ken Gray Filters Sales and Service. You have the warehouse, two trucks. And you call on hospitals, pharmaceuticals and plants locally. And you would buy our products and sell our products. So that's the third space. And, you know, we had the high purity space, which is HEPA filtration, clean room filtration and nuclear filtration. And then, you know, we had a complete service division, which was rooftop change outs, mostly big box stores, so forth and so on. And we also had a paint booth division. So the paint booth division would sell paint booth and roll type products to, you know, automobile dealerships and so forth. And so, you know, what I learned quickly was it was a pretty complex model. And so I really ingrained myself into learning, who, what, when where and how from a competitive landscape. So I would say, yeah, I got up to speed really, really quickly on -- on all the divisions.

Q: Okay. Let me go through --
A: And I'm sorry, retail as well.
08_chunk_0005.title: 08 (chunk 6/56)

08_chunk_0006.text:
where and how from a competitive landscape. So I would say, yeah, I got up to speed really, really quickly on -- on all the divisions.

Q: Okay. Let me go through --
A: And I'm sorry, retail as well.

Q: Yeah. Retail, explain that. And basically explain what Flanders does.
A: Sure. Yeah. So Flanders Corporation, you know, is a multi-faceted air filtration company. What I got at Flanders Corporation is an evolution of the model. So when I got to Flanders Corporation it was in financial challenge. It's public record was a NASDAQ traded company. So what my thesis when they offered me -- took the job, was that we had a model problem. Because, you know, we had the direct offices I was telling you about, and then, you know, we also sold to Ken Gray Filter Sales and Service. So you would actually go and compete with our direct offices every day. So we'd have sales guys on our payroll competing with you selling our products. And the same thing in the retail space. Instead of you going to Lowe's, you could just go to one of our direct offices and buy our filters. So, you know, what I said is we had a confused strategy. And what we had at that time was a CEO that was buying (indiscernible.) So I mean, he was losing market share in the normalized market because people didn't trust us as a partner, because we were competing with him. So he was going out and buying Ken Gray's Air Filter Service. So, you know, you say, hey, I'll sell it. I do 8 million in sales. And then, you know, we buy it and it looks like you've got $8 million in revenue growth. And so, you know, we had a very challenged balance sheet. We had a loss in customer base and we had poor service because, you know, we had financial challenges, raw material flows, so forth and so on. So when I got in the company, you know, I said, I'm going to take it here. So where I took it to was strictly in the direction -- so I spun off all the direct offices, sold them all off to Ken Gray. So, you know, I said, Ken, would you like to have two more offices? And I worked with our existing filter sales and service space to -- to buy those branches and incorporate the trust that we weren't going to compete with you. And then we put the -- we spun off the complete service division, which was the rooftops, you know, because we were competing as well there. So we got out of that space. We got out of the paint booth space because it just wasn't a core space, it was a cash burner. We had a competing high purity plant in Salt Lake City, Utah, which is where the former CEO lived. So we had a competing plant to the high purity plant in Washington. So they actually had a sales force in Salt Lake City. We had a sales force in Washington. Didn't work out so good. We competed for price. So you could call Salt Lake City and get a price for a HEPA filter and you could call Washington for a price for a HEPA filter. And so I shut that plant down. And we had a detached corporate office, which doesn't work for a company in this space. So the detached corporate office was in Florida, which the ex-CEO had a place in as well. And I closed it down and I moved the corporate office to Washington, North Carolina. Two fronts there, one, job creation in North Carolina, which was near and dear to me. Didn't try to hide that. And, two, I wanted to be with my family. I didn't want to be in Florida. And so, you know, we took a detached office, the detached corporate office and moved it to Washington, North Carolina, which would be customer service, accounting, IT and all those platforms. In that process, the world said you can't hire enough help in Washington, North Carolina. We had all the help we wanted, great folks, and it worked really, really well. That was when the company started turning. We took a tremendous amount of overhead out and then, you know, we really started driving service through efficiency and trust. The retail space is a very difficult. In and to itself, it's a tough space. You know, you're calling on Wal-Mart, Lowe's and Home Depot. And it's really a two-edged sword, you know. I can also tell you, if I go back into this, I don't know that I'm going into that space. I still have a lot of friends there, but why did I have a lot of friends? I couldn't run a company without them. So, you know, we were approximately -- these are rough numbers. I think when I got it, we were probably 160, 165 million, you know. When I exited we were 325, something like that.

And at that same period in the turnaround, I ended up with all the real estate. So we'll explain how I ended up in the real estate business. We didn't have any capital. So Bartow burned to the ground. That was a manufacturing plant in Florida. Key and critical plant because Florida's hot and we sell a lot of filters there. So we had an old plant and had a guy -- a man and his wife, as I recall, burned the plant down. Air filters burned. So burned the plant down. I immediately went back to Bank of America, who was -- we had our ABL, which was asset based lending, you know. We borrowed money off of receivables and inventory and balance sheet. And we were leveraged. I mean every week I was paying, you know, payroll. I got company with no cash. So I went to the Bank of America and sat down with Bob Rhodes and Bob Moore, two great guys who I still think a lot of today. And I said, I need -- I need to rebuild Bartow. And as I recall, Bob Rhodes started laughing. He said, here, come on. What's the next conversation? I said, I've got to -- I mean I'm done if I can't rebuild this plant. I had the dirt because I owned the dirt. And the said, we're not going to let you -- no more debt for this company. We're not going to get more exposure. We're not going to allow the company to have anymore exposure. I didn't understand it then. I understand it now. I mean it was back -- I was still -- when I was -- I mean -- so I called Robert. And, you know, Robert had some net worth, right. And I said, look, I've got to rebuild this plant. And he said, okay, well, let's rebuild it. So he and I went to BB&T, back when you could borrow money you shouldn't be able to borrow. And he and I bought the land from the company, fair market appraisal, you know, arm's length transaction, fully documented and vetted, gave the company a 1.5, $2 million injection of cash, which helped the company. And so you're going to get a turnaround at the time we turned this thing around here in a second. And then we borrowed, I think 7 to $9 million and built the plant ourselves. So we owned Bartow. That's how the real estate function started for me.

The brought us Honeywell Rehm, which gave us national branding for the first time ever. And we actually negotiated an open, transparent return. And, you know, we went to -- we probably had three points in profit on Home Depot until we moved to ten in total transparency. And that year we were supplier of the year for Home Depot and vendor of the year for Home Depot.

And that is what Bank of America recommended to me as a young, inexperienced CEO. They said, Harry, you need to put this in bankruptcy. You can't fix this. I said, guys, I'm going to give it a shot. But keep in mind the driving premise of that is I had borrowed $3.5 million. So, you know, it's not that -- that was my driving premise for not putting it in bankruptcy. So today if you brought me in, with the skill set I have today, I'd say, Ken, that's the very best thing we can do. Your balance sheet's shot. You know, you've got model problems. Let's reorganize, shrink the company and then start regrowing, total transparency. I would not put the company through the moves that I put it through. And I don't think many people would. I mean it really impacted my health and -- and -- but I was somewhat trapped. And so, thus, also the desire to exit when I exited.

Q: You were trapped because you had put in your own money, right?

A: Correct.

Q: So that --

I could take the company private myself, and I had the option to do that. Or I could sell it. And I did not want to take the company private for the things I had told you before. My concern was with the model. And so we put a book together and hired an M and A firm and went out and met with 25 or 30 different potential buyers. And Insight was the high bidder. And we went back and forth with them and were able to get a transaction done, and all the shareholders were happy. So we, you know, moved the company to ownership structure of Insight and Harry.

Q: Okay. Now, let me ask you this. You said all of the shareholders were happy. Would these be shareholders of the private entity at this point?
A: Right. So when we went from NASDAQ to pink sheets, your shares still move. So you know, we had mutual funds and we had embodiment of shareholders. And so we were able to negotiate a price that everybody said, okay, we're -- you know, we're happy and, you know, we're able to move it through that next phase, which is somewhat untypical that you don't incur any significant losses in that process.

Q: And so when Insight came in, were there additional shares issued?

Q: It was Insight Equity Holdings --

Q: -- and Harry Smith?

And so I'll leave a portion in but, you know, I'm going to take a portion work. If that doesn't work and that doesn't work. I had already sold all our real estates. I had gotten off of that risk.

Q: Okay. Let's -- then let's back up. The real estate that you owned that you sold, what was that?
A: That was the plants that we had talked about earlier that I sold.

Q: And did you sell them all to one buyer?
A: Sold every one of them to W.P. Carey out of New York, a REAT. So I went to the Board --

Q: Can you spell Carey?
A: It's C-A-R-E-Y.

Q: And it's a REAT?
A: It's a REAT. And the individual I dealt with was a guy name Gino Sabatini, who is still there.

Q: And the REIT bought a hundred percent of the real property that you had owned --
A: For the company.

Q: -- for the company?
A: Right. And, you know, when you're public, you know, all this is full disclosure. So we had to disclose, you know, everything from lease, rents, market. Then we had to do market valuation and everything has to be arm's length, you know. But it turned out to be a really great deal for me, but it could have turned out to be a really bad deal. So I mean it was a Catch 22 until I got the company turned. And as soon as I got the company on a stable platform, I went to exit mode, which also means I wanted off the real estate. And so, I think Christian was a big adviser for me then, Ken, Christian Porter. And so I went to the Board and said, look, I'm over exposed here. It's time for me to mitigate risk. You know, the company's doing well. And so we took the -- we ratified the leases and took it to market and I -- and I mitigated that risk with W.P. Carey. And really from a balance standpoint, it's really much more balanced to have the insider transactions like that. I did it because I was forced to have to rebuild it. So I exited, and it turned out to be -- to be a solid exit for me.

oint, it's really much more balanced to have the insider transactions like that. I did it because I was forced to have to rebuild it. So I exited, and it turned out to be -- to be a solid exit for me.

And Robert was trying to figure out how to get the family that had found it, Flanders in Washington, out. And Steve was more of a whiz Wall Street type of guy, actually a very brilliant guy finance-wise, but not so much operations-wise. So Steve was the guy that everything he was going to do was going to work and he went all in. And he didn't really measure and moderate his decisions, but a very smart guy. He talked Robert into the fact that he could take the company public, raise a lot of money, buy up some people and exit. They took the company public, raised 30 or 60 million in their first offering, bought Precision Air, bought Air Seal. They bought a commodity of air filtration companies, put it together, and it never performed. So it's the classic example of raising capital and overpaying. So, you know, he raised capital and overpaid to employ capital.

A: He was granted stock, yeah. I don't -- to my knowledge, I don't know of Steve ever buying a share.

A: Not that I recall. I was gifted one million shares by the Board.

A: I don't recall buying any. I was gifted a million shares and I also had options that, if I recall, were probably 250,000 shares. But I was gifted one million at zero consideration.

A: I did exercise those.

Q: Okay.
A: Right.

Q: All right.
A: Yes.

A: I'd say two years into my CEO leadership role, Ken. And how that went down is we had a Board meeting, and I had, in my opinion, significantly overpaid for the shares I bought. I think I had to back that in detail to prove that it was not worth 3.5 million when I bought them.

Q: You're talking about when you bought Clark shares?
A: Clark shares, right. And I basically went in and said, guys, you know, I took on significant risk here. You know, I was not knowledgeable. I am now. This is what I really think it was worth. I think they agreed. And I said, This is what I want in consideration of me putting my family at risk, me at risk and my health at risk. And I said, I'm asking for a million shares.

Q: Okay. So let's go back. Because I guess you did buy some shares when you bought Clark out?
A: I did buy six shares, correct.

Q: Because by that time you had sold the real estate and --
A: And I had also gotten into the multi- family business and I had hit it right on time. So, you know, the first two complexes I bought, you know, were in bankruptcy, great recession. And, you know, I paid five and ended up selling 17 and 18. So I mean I had built some wealth there.

Q: But Insight's the one that ended up buying Robert Amerson out?
A: And myself, except what I kept in, correct. Insight took everybody out but me.

A: I don't recall the transaction amount. We sold at 4.25 a share, approximately, something like that, 4.28, if I remember correctly.
