And then I took that portion and paid off my original 3.5 million. And then the bulk of my gain was the million shares that I was gifted in my options. There was no gain on the shares I bought from Steve Clark. In fact, I actually, if I remember correctly, lost money because of the interest I paid on the $3.5 million. So my gain became the million shares that I was gifted and the 250 shares that I sold, as well as, you know, I had a significant income period there from -- from rent and W-2. So I was making approximately a million to 1,250,000 a year, you know, to run the company, compensation and bonuses. And then, you know, I had the rent on top of that. So I mean my income, you know, at that time, including the multi-family, I was probably making $3.5 million a year.

Q: The multi-family, though, is not related?
A: Not related. I mean that was --

Q: So if you took that out --
A: Yeah, probably $2 million a year.

Q: Two million dollars from your compensation, the -- and the amount that you were renting to the company?
A: Uh-huh. That's correct. Yeah, that's correct. And then -- so, yeah, I had built some significant wealth there. And I had built enough wealth that, you know, I didn't want to continue to push in. I wanted to push out. And so -- and was pretty tired and wanted to do some other things. And I was very upfront with Insight about all that. I said, guys, this is where I'm at. I'm not going to be a long-term player for you. This is my recommendation that you buy this company. Let me rev revenues up, really increase sales, drive EBITDA as hard as we can, and you guys should exit. And I'll exit with you, but I want to go ahead and slide backwards. I don't want to be the guy on the front of the exit. That was our plan when they bought the company.

A: No. I mean their goal was -- and I made a commitment to stay with them. Now, listen, I learned a lot about private equity on leverage. Q: . So, Mr. Smith, we were getting into talking about Insight. So, could you tell us how that came into being?
A: . Sure. We took the company to market and I think we showed it to 25 to 30 different buyers, would have been strategic buyers and also would have been financial buyers, Insight being a financial buyer. Insight was the high bid. We took it and we actually out of showing it to 30 qualified buyers we actually had two offers total in the corporation. So, not a lot of interest.

Q: . Insight was the high bid and the Board accepted Insight's bid?
A: . Correct.

Q: . What role did Insight want you to have?
A: . Chief Executive Officer and I was a member of the Board as well.

Q: . And was it still Flanders Corporation?
A: . Correct, Flanders Corp.

Q: . Do you recall when this sale occurred?
A: . It's public record I -- if I recall was August 2015 or something -- no, '14, in that time period. '13, '14, I'm terrible on that stuff, but I mean it's public record.

Q: . Did you execute a separation agreement at that time?
A: . I executed a long term incentive compensation plan, and I don't actually recall all that I executed. Obviously it was a tremendous amount of documents at that time. The one document I do remember was the long term incentive compensation plan that they offered me.

Q: . Was your role changing in any way?
A: . No. I was no longer Chairman of the Board but I was still CEO and a member of the Board.

Q: . Were you just regular member or were you Vice Chair?
A: . No, I was just a regular member of the Board.

Q: . Okay. And you believe that was the summer of 2014?
A: . Somewhere in that time period.

Q: . How did things progress from that point forward?
A: . I would think it probably progressed as typical fashion, a middle market company that gets over leveraged. So, what was unique in this process was when I sold to Insight, they told me that they did not take distributions, that I never had to worry about giving a distribution to Insight. So, they did put a lot of leverage on it including mezzanine debt, which I understood when we closed. Approximately 90 days into the close I was contacted by the CEO and Chairman of Insight and he asked me for a $7,000,000 distribution.

Q: . And just to be clear for the record, earlier we were talking about distribution and that was we were talking about selling product --
A: . Product.

Q: . -- to a customer. Now when you're talking about distribution, you're talking more in terms of a dividend?
A: . Correct. So, he contacted me and it was early on, 90 to 120 days, if I remember correctly, I think that's approximately, and asked me to come up with a $7,000,000 distribution to Insight.

Q: . Who was this person?
A: . It would have been Ted Beneski, the CEO of Insight and the founder of Insight. I was taken back. My CFO John Oakley who had been with the through the entire process was taken back. We kind of came back and holed up and there was absolutely no way I could do it. The balance sheet was incredibly stressed. I would have had to gone back to early days. And so, I basically went back and said absolutely impossible. And then I think there was a little bit of a friction based on that. But I'm pretty good with balance sheets and income statements, there was just absolutely no way I could figure out how to do that.

08_chunk_0024.text:

A: . Correct.

Q: . Okay. So, he was Chair of both.
A: . Correct.

Q: . And so you told him you couldn't do it?
A: . Couldn't do it.

Q: . And the CFO you're referring to is John Oakley?
A: . Correct. Correct.

Q: . Now, explain why because if you say we can't do it, then --
A: . John basically came in and he had done fairly well in the sale of the company. I don't know exactly what his gain was but probably, you know, a couple million dollars approximately. And he just said this isn't going to work. I don't want to go back down this road, and I need to go. And I think that set the path for some of the challenges because John was a very -- he'd managed the balance sheet with me a long. But he exited, that was the premise of the exit. I'm going to say that was the complete exit but that started the -- him having a very difficult relationship with Insight.

Q: . And just to be clear, how much did you make on the sale?
A: . On the sale of the company? On the original stock I bought I lost money. So, my original investment of three and a half million I lost. The shares that I was awarded, you know, I made whatever we sold the company for. And then I kept $660,000 in at par value of the sale. So, it'd been what we got at the sale price and the valuation on that I think they had it at $1 share so they redid the valuation. But I kept $660,000 in approximately. So, the 660 was what I left in based on the price that they sold at -- they bought us at.

Q: . Did you mention earlier that you thought the price per share was 28?
A: . No, it was -- it was probably 4.28 or something like that. You know, we sold for approximately 200,000,000, 225,000,000 but that includes debt, you know, everything that goes along with it.

Q: . But $428 per share?
A: . No, no, no, $4.28.

Q: . Okay, yeah. So, basically you could multiply --
A: . It's all public record.

Q: . Right, 4.28 times a million and that would be what you received?
A: . Correct, right. Well, when I had my final exit, I had no gain. So, I actually had wanted to leave my shares in and they wanted me to go ahead and completely get out of the ownership structure. So, they forced me out. I knew the value of the company was much higher at that time because we had grown $100 million. And Insight basically said you know what, if you want to exit, that's fine, then you can't be an owner. And part of the exit they forced the sale of my 660,000 shares at significantly below market. So, you know, I left a significant amount of money on the table from my shares. So, if you would calculate the value I had grown the company to, you know, the overall transaction I lost money. So, you know, I grew the company $100 million from the time Insight bought it till they exited and so your valuation jumps significantly. And so, I actually said Brad, my share is worth a lot more than this and they would only give me par value on the exit. And so, it was kind of, you know, some pretension there, and I actually exited at a significant loss, you know, when I sold my 660,000 because I didn't get any gain on it at all based on two and a half, three years of immense amount of work and moving the valuation of the company. So, you know, if you look at company valuations, you know, we grew $100 million in my last tenure there before I exited. I got no -- I got no return on that at all. I was vested in my long term incentive compensation plan. So, if you go back and look at the paperwork, I had a significant long term incentive compensation plan that was extremely generous because they wanted to retain me. And so, I was vested. Even if I exited and walked out the door, I was contractually vested in the gain of the company. When I exited, I voluntarily gave up the long term incentive compensation plan with the written request and verbal request that that went to my employees. The value of that I think was probably $5,000,000,000 that I -- that I -- when I left, my request was that it went to the employees of Flanders Corporation. I had done really well and it was a pretty emotional exit. And but I voluntarily gave up the LTIC. Victor Vescovo called me and said this is the first time in history I've ever seen anything like that. But I voluntarily gave that up and the request was it went to Flanders Corporation. And I don't know that they honored that but I made that request to Victor and Brad that my LTIC would be awarded upon the sale of the company and at that time I mean Victor even said Harry, do you know what this is worth and I said I do. So, I was trying to exit with the best, you know, premise in mind. The history on that, as you know, you know, I went to the Board, we brought Peter Jones in. Peter was not a great hire and Insight agreed with me. The CFO actually called for his termination. I stepped in and mitigated that. The biggest mistake I made was when I returned.

ght Peter Jones in. Peter was not a great hire and Insight agreed with me. The CFO actually called for his termination. I stepped in and mitigated that. The biggest mistake I made was when I returned.

A: . Uh-huh. Yes.

Q: . And at what point did Peter Jones come into the picture?
A: . Great. So, some history there I don't remember the exact dynamic, probably 18 months in. So, how did Peter Jones come into the picture. So, it made MERV six, seven, and eight media and it made the electrostatic media for Home Depot. What happened to bring Peter Jones in, there's a company called Blackstone, and Blackstone had a $15,000,000 mezz strip with us at 18 percent -- it may have been 20,000,000 but they had a mezz strip. And Blackstone owned the company called PGI Industries and PGI Industries made MERV six, seven, and eight media. So, we were moving the buy to Pronamics with Insight's support. And they were trying to sell PGI Industries. And Brad Coleman, who was the lead guy at Blackstone who I met with, we went up, we had put the company in a tremendous growth curve -- $100 million in probably six months. We took on Home Depot nationwide, took on Grainger, 4,000 new part numbers overnight. I think we hired four to 500 people. We have to buy five, six, $7 million of equipment to service it with. So, big dynamic change to the company, right? I flew to Texas. I said guys -- with the CFO, who was Scott Brown, I said guys, this is the dynamic change I talked to you about. You know, the company's going to through a curve, we're going to get insufficient, we've got 4,000 new part numbers, we've got to hire new people. So, we're going to go through a curve with EBITDA, you know, we're going to come out here and we were here. But we're going to dip and I need capital. So, we started the dip and it was pretty a pretty stressful time when you went from 225 to 335. Those are pretty close variables. I got no working capital. So, they gave me $5 million at a bullet at high interest. So, Brad Coleman really started getting over involved and at the same he started putting pressure on us to PGI, who they owned as a portfolio company. And we had the conversations internally with Insight and Brad Coleman was just continuing to step in. He was calling me direct. I thought it was, you know, very inappropriate. We had a much lower price than PGI was giving us internally. Long story short I got sideways with Brad Coleman and Coleman threatened Insight to pull it. Brad Coleman--

Q: . And when you say pull it, you mean pull the loan --
A: . Right.

Q: . -- and call -- and make a call?
A: . Right. Victor Vescovo and the Board at the Bartow plant internally and Victor said, Harry, we've lost our soul to the bank. Right? And I said okay and he said, you know, Brad is -- we can't afford to lose Blackstone in our bigger organization. We need you to step back and go to the Board and let us bring in a guy that you work with because you and Brad, you know, are butting heads. I said that's fine, I don't have any problem with that. And so, we actually -- that's how Peter Jones came in. We had a great meeting in Bartow. I said I'll go to the Board, which really worked for me. So, I went to the Board, we brought Peter in. Peter had been unemployed approximately seven to eight years. He was -- from a dynamic standpoint it was a big mistake. Insight will tell you that today. Brad and Victor will both tell you he was a full British accent going to Home Depot just doesn't work, right? So, I was at the Board and pretty happy and really was this is myself. Brad Coleman stepped in and started a full blown attack on Pronamics to get PGI back the media business. So, I had invested in Pronamics for Insight at Insight's request everything like we had said and we were going to use the Pronamics piece in the sale. So, when we were looking at selling the company, we were going to roll Pronamics in so they vertical supply on the raw materials side.

08_chunk_0026.text:
ad said and we were going to use the Pronamics piece in the sale. So, when we were looking at selling the company, we were going to roll Pronamics in so they vertical supply on the raw materials side.

Q: . Okay. Let me stop you there. The plan at that moment was that obviously since this was a private equity firm they want to flip this thing, they want to get it --
A: . Correct.

Q: . -- get in a position where it could sell it for a profit and the plan was that you were going to be the CEO until that occurred?
A: . Uh-huh. Yes.

Q: . And that Pronamics, which you and the other two guys still owned, was going to be part of that deal as well as Flanders?
A: . Correct. So, we were going to be vertical in the raw materials side with technology. So, there was only one other superior -- there was only one other fiberglass supplier in the country and they had a catastrophic events. So, we were controlling the supply chain with fiberglass, too, and we had all our internal consumption and we had put together a robust research and development team on the media side. So, we opened a plant in Wilson and that's where the media was made, and we have a plant in Washington where the fiberglass was made. All ground zero build ups. So, I go to the Board and Brad Coleman immediately starts putting pressure -- because the procurement guys I would come into the plant and the procurement guys would say hey, Harry, can we talk to you. And I'd go in there and they said hey, we just had to call this Brad Coleman guy from PGI, he's trying -- from Blackstone, he wants us to buy from PGI, we don't know what to do. I said well, you need to buy from the lowest cost producer. If that's not Pronamics, you shouldn't do it I mean because -- but I also knew he couldn't get there, we didn't have no overhead. Long story short Insight called me and said we've got to do something here, we can't lose the Blackstone relationship. But Brad Coleman from Blackstone forced my exit to the Board. Now, what Victor Vescovo said is look, we're going to play this game, we want to put you back in the CEO role when we go to sale because at that point we're close enough that we can -- you and Brad can work it out if he thinks he's going to get a return. My comment was let's get there and see how that works. I was great with Peter, didn't have a problem with Peter at all. Peter came in immediately. Travis Stephenson can attest to this one, about 30 days in he calls me in and goes Insight's made a massive mistake buying this company. I said, really. He said, they've made a massive mistake, I want to scare the shit out of him - excuse me, what he told me - and get them out. They said I'm going to talk them in to taking a loss. I said, Peter, that's a mistake. I said, you know, we're scaling. So, Peter had never run a company probably with more than 100 employees. I said, Peter, I think that's incorrect from a valuation standpoint. You know, I saw it where it was going. He was struggling, the CFO Scott Brown actually called Insight and the Board and called for his termination. His exact words was he can't do this, he can't lead us, he's in over his head. I stepped in, calmed all that down, went to Costa Rica fishing. Victor and Brad called me. I was over there and we had a three-hour phone call where they put a tremendous amount of pressure on me to come back as the Managing Director of Flanders. I pushed against it. I fought against. And long story short, I went back as a Managing Director with Peter reporting to me.

Q: . Now, explain that dynamic because at that point is Peter the CE --
A: . Peter was the CEO and I was just a Board member.

Q: . But you were called a Managing Director?
A: . They called me back as the Managing Director. We still had this dynamic with Brad Coleman at Blackstone. So, right -- and

Q: . So, you couldn't officially be --
A: . You know, look, I could have sued Blackstone coming and going and I had all the facts down in detail. Because as soon as Brad Coleman forced Flanders to move the media business back to PGI they sold the business. So, I mean they were trying to run revenues up on Flanders and Brad Coleman was using their ownership structure and its overall strength in that industry to pressure Flanders to do. It was pretty grotesque and Insight was really worried about it because they, you know -- and I said guys, let's just keep working. Right. But I came back as a Managing Director, basically took over. Peter the first -- the first day back in Peter came to me and said would you buy the company back if I talked Ted into taking a $50 million loss. And I said no. He said can talk him into short selling this company back to you, we've made a mistake. At the same time Insight had a company called EMES, that's its public trader ticker, okay. It was a sand play and it was trading at approximately $140 a share. In that same conversation Peter Jones looked at me and said I'm on the Board over there, and this thing's an operational disaster, and Insight's looking for a win anywhere they can get it. This thing, you know, we're going to get in trouble because of the valuation of this stock. And I was like Peter, I ain't got nothing to do with that. I said I want to help Insight exit. So, that kind of continued to -- it was just constant every day. At the same time when I came back, you know, I became under a tremendous attack from a small group of employees that did not want me to reenter the space, right? So, you know, I came back, I was pretty strong leader. I was looking, you know, where I could drive. I cut benefits pretty quickly trying to drive EBITDA. And I came under a pretty vicious attack. Case in point was the Beaufort Observer, you know, wrote a scathing piece on me that had all kinds of context written into it. I didn't respond to it at all and they actually contacted me, called me said, are you going to respond to this. I said, no, I understand but it's all incorrect. He said, can I come to talk to you and I said, sure. He came sat down, we gave him the fact, Brad gave him all the Board minutes everything we'd done on Pronamics everything, investment, what was going on with Peter. We put all the facts out there, he wrote a full redaction and apology. He also in that thing said there's four or five people that are Flanders that are writing all this stuff. And I said, I understand. At the same time, you know, I had hacked email issues that, you know, because I was going in my personal email. So, there was a personal attack within the company in a small group. But it put a lot of pressure on me, you know, at home and everything else. Now, I understood it and I told Insight I understood it. And, you know, I actually sent some emails to Insight asking specific people to stop writing because we knew who they were. I didn't fire them, but we knew who they were. And so, you know, I endeared a very personal attack when I came back as managing director from a small group of people both internal and external. And so, I was dealing with all of that at the same time. And that's culminated the final exit was Peter Jones asking to buy the company back. The other thing that happened when I came back as managing director was Insight asked me to sign the bank line. So, the bank came in with Scott Brown and I, we were trying to renew a current bank line that we had. And the bank said we're not going to renew it because you're too leveraged. We will renew it if Harry signs a personal guarantee. I mean, I had tons of cash, big balance sheet. Insight got me on the phone and said we need you to sign this personal guarantee. I said, guys, I'm a minority shareholder and this -- you got this -- so that was the dynamic. They were trying to force me to sign a personal guarantee with the bank which is one of the reasons that I sold the company. So, I just said, that's it, it's time. You know, I've got to go. And I had sold the media plant to SWM, a publicly traded company and sold the glass plant to Flanders and exited. So, you know, went to the Board, brought me back as managing director. I don't remember the compensation. It was a crazy number they paid me to come back. You can go dig it up, they've got it I'm sure. They paid me an enormous amount of money to come back and threw everything I wanted at me. I mean I could -- whatever I wanted they said yeah. And so, I stepped back in running it, the dynamics were just incredible. There was two different camps. So, you had the camp that Peter developed when he came in because he had his own guys. So, you know, my guys were over here and all the sudden we went from one organization that was, you know, a North Carolina based driven company to, you know, we had this camp that didn't want Harry back, right? So, we had hired Nevin Caldwell, who'd been unemployed for a significant of time as a chief operating officer. We had hired Ron Shriver who had been unemployed for a significant period of time, you know. So, we had this group of people that had gotten into a significant position of power. We're looking at an LTIC and you had that dynamic. I gave it the best run I could. I had already sold Pronamics, that transaction was done. Insight, Flanders Corporation bought the glass plant, I'd sold that. I came back and I gave it everything I could and it just wouldn't work. So, you know, that precipitated the exit. And when I exited, you know, I think I left -- if you would count the valuation of what the shares that I short sold for and my long incentive compensation plan, I think you could quantify seven to $8 million that I gave up to be able to exit the company without creating any angst. And I exited very quietly. I continued to work with Insight with customers. I went to Home Depot I think twice on my own accord, my own ticket, and continued to say, you know, stay with these guys, work with them. Insight called me once a week. Peter Jones, you know, came to my son's football game to get advice. One of the things that concerned Insight when I had finally decided I was going to exit because at some point you got to go -- Home Depot actually flew in and met with me, Brad, and he told Brad if he exits, we've lost trust, I don't think you'll see a single source. And my advice to Insight was to exit. My advice also when American Air was looking at my Insight was to make sure full disclosure on the fragility of the retail piece of business. Because I perceived it to be fragile and I thought that they should be aware of that. So, but I continued to help Insight and Peter, you know, for a significant period of time with customers, vendors. And, you know, and I think you could easily quantify that I gave up seven to $8 million when I exited. And I knew that. I mean I knew what my long term incentive compensation was worth. I knew my shares were worth a significant amount more. And I had done really well and I didn't want to exit with that approach. And I think Insight will tell you, you know, it was one of the most gracious things they've ever seen. My hope is it went to the employees. That was the request.

Q: . Just tell me real quick.
A: . Sure. Yeah, Oak Ridge -- Insight came to us early on and, you know, we had an internal machine shop with -- where we machined all our own parts internally. And one of their first requests is that we exit the machine shop business and procure the parts. And so, Kevin Boyd, who had ran the machine shop and was a key and integral part player, called me and said, look, these are 20-year guys, 25-year guys, is there anything we can do. And he said -- I said, you know, let me talk to Brad. I called Brad and I said, look, you know, we hate to send these people home, they're eastern North Carolina, and they've been with us and, you know, part of this deal was, you know, we're going to grow, not hurt. And I said, you know, what can we do. He called me back and said, look, you know, if you guys would like to buy the assets and hire those employers, we would work out an agreement where you guys could open a business. We would still procure those parts at a competitive price which means you'd get more bids, but that would be an opportunity, that's the only thing we can do. And he said, by the way, that'd be a big win for us because we don't know if we could sell the equipment, which was fair. We went and got an arm's length valuation on all the equipment and we entered into an agreement to buy the equipment and we also entered into an agreement with the company with Insight managing that process on where we got first right of refusal on machine work within the company. And as a part of that process Kevin had developed an automation program, two different types of products called Pac and C-Pac, which took out a lot of the labor, and he had developed it in-house. And they also driven by Brad Buser and Eliot Kerlin wanted Oak Ridge to build I think six of those machines. So, that is what started Oak Ridge. You know, I went in with Kevin 50/50 and it was Kevin's venture. Kevin now owns it 100 percent. So, we went and bought a building, put him in it, hired all the employees, nobody lost their job, and we put them in business. I covered all the capital losses. We had a capital loss the first two or three years where we lost, you know, money and all that's of record as well. I covered the losses until Kevin got stabilized and then I gave Kevin the business at no consideration. So, Oak Ridge is still performing today. You know, one of the points of contention that we had talked about before was immediately when we doing -- Oak Ridge was doing a significant amount of business with Flanders and Insight was also contacted Kevin and said we want you to do business with our other companies. You've done a really good job, you've built every single piece of equipment in the company. As soon as Daikin took over the POs stopped and communication to Flanders was we've been given -- and need not to do business with you. So, Kevin didn't understand it. Kevin tried to contact Howard Campbell, who as I understand it was terminated by Phil Whitaker, that's what we were told. And, you know, the word to the corporation is we're not allowed to buy from you. Kevin reached out, sent multiple emails, said can I help, I want to help. It was not antagonistical, he had a great relationship with Insight working in the plants all the time. And he lost a significant amount of business day one that Daikin took over and we never understood. And then we started getting feedback. Kevin had also built the glass plant, which was directly across the street from Oak Ridge, I mean they're across the street from each other. He designed it, built it, bought equipment and immediately as well because, you know, that was part of it. Insight said we want -- that business stopped as well. And as well, you know, there was comments coming out right, wrong, or indifferent that were pretty derogatory. But there was -- never should have -- I mean Kevin never did anything in any way, shape, form, or fashion to be retaliated like that. And I mean it -- the business stopped immediately. And this was a process where we saved jobs in eastern North Carolina, made a significant investment in the east, and bought an empty building. And look, that business is flourishing today and providing a lot of jobs in the east. And I've got to tell you when -- when Phil Whitaker who said that he'd made a decision not to do that, and Kevin sent multiple emails said just let me help you and he could have helped him dramatically, he really harmed eastern North Carolina and I injected a lot of capital to cover Oak Ridge as Kevin developed other customers. So, that is how Oak Ridge was formed and it's flourishing and doing really well today.

med eastern North Carolina and I injected a lot of capital to cover Oak Ridge as Kevin developed other customers. So, that is how Oak Ridge was formed and it's flourishing and doing really well today.

It's one of the most key raw materials suppliers. What I was trying to do here was do the right thing. A: . I wasn't under attack, my guys weren't under attack, and I wasn't getting calls from customers, vendors, and employees, people had not lost their job as a result of alignment with me. So, that was not an issue. I will testify again I have no desire to go back in the air filtration business in in any way, shape, form, or fashion.

Q: . So, the answer is no, it was not important at that time?
A: . Absolutely not. I will also say as far as an air filtration start up I mean, you know, I'm three years now so I got two years left, 24 months and now really isn't going to make any difference if they don't change the model. But what I will you is no matter what the court decides if something doesn't change course, Kevin and Travis are going to reenter the space. Their non-competes are clear and they going to have the same kind of impact. I don't know the magnitude of the impact, but I think those guys will have a significant impact whether I'm involved or not. So, you know, Travis and Kevin are completely cleared and I think you'll see unless something changes, those guys will enter the space and -- on their own without me in any way, shape, form, or fashion. That's I think -- I think that's what will happen if something doesn't change course. MR. GRAY: Anything else? MR. CEGLOWSKI: No. MR. GRAY: Let's go off the record.
